docs.title: Q1. What is an exception in Java?
docs.text:
An exception is an event that interrupts the normal flow of program execution.

Example:

```java int result = 10 / 0; ```

This causes ArithmeticException.

docs.text:
Exception handling is a mechanism used to handle runtime problems without abruptly terminating the application.

⬆ Back to Questions

docs.title: Q3. What is the exception hierarchy?
docs.text:
The root class of Java exceptions and errors is Throwable.

It has two main subclasses:

  • Exception
  • Error

docs.text:
Checked exceptions are checked by the compiler.

Unchecked exceptions occur at runtime.

docs.title: Java Exception Handling
docs.text:
Understand exception handling from basic to advanced concepts.

Topic

Core Java | Exception Handling | Interview Preparation

docs.title: Q1. What is an exception in Java?
docs.text:
Basic

An exception is an unexpected event that occurs during program execution and interrupts the normal flow of instructions.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
public class ExceptionExample {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        int result = 10 / 0;

        System.out.println(result);
    }
}

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text: The above program throws ArithmeticException because integer division by zero is not allowed.

docs.title: Interview Tip
docs.text: Explain that exceptions represent abnormal conditions that an application can handle.

docs.title: Q2. What is exception handling?
docs.text:
Basic

Exception handling is the mechanism used to detect and handle runtime problems so that an application can respond appropriately.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
public class ExceptionHandlingExample {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        try {
            int result = 10 / 0;
            System.out.println(result);
        } catch (ArithmeticException exception) {
            System.out.println("Cannot divide by zero");
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Interview Tip
docs.text: Explain try, catch, finally, throw and throws.

docs.title: Q3. Why do we need exception handling?
docs.text:
Basic

Exception handling helps applications:

  1. Prevent unexpected termination where recovery is possible.
  2. Maintain application stability.
  3. Separate business logic from error-handling logic.
  4. Provide meaningful error messages.
  5. Support proper logging and debugging.

docs.title: Q4. What is the difference between Exception and Error?
docs.text:
Intermediate

Exception Error Usually represents conditions an application may handle. Usually represents serious system or JVM problems. Can be checked or unchecked. Generally unchecked. Examples: IOException, SQLException. Examples: OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError.

docs.title: Q5. Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions
docs.text:
Intermediate

Checked Unchecked Checked at compile time. Not checked at compile time. Must be caught or declared. No mandatory catch or declaration. IOException NullPointerException SQLException ArithmeticException

docs.title: Q6. Java Exception Hierarchy
docs.text:
Advanced

Object
  |
Throwable
  |
  +--- Error
  |
  +--- Exception
         |
         +--- RuntimeException
         |
         +--- IOException
         |
         +--- SQLException

Advanced Interview Tip

Explain Throwable, Exception, RuntimeException and Error with practical examples.

docs.title: 1.1 What is Dirty Checking?
docs.text:
Dirty Checking is a Hibernate mechanism that automatically detects changes made to a managed entity and generates the required UPDATE SQL query when the transaction is flushed.

In simple words: - Fetch an employee from the database. - Change the employee's name. - Don't call repository.save(). - Hibernate automatically detects the change. - Hibernate generates an UPDATE query during flush/commit.

This is called Dirty Checking.

docs.title: 1.2 How does Dirty Checking work?
docs.text:
Suppose we have an Employee table:

Initial Database State (employee table):

id name salary 101 Rahul 30000 102 Amit 40000

Now we want to change Rahul's salary from ₹30,000 to ₹50,000. Hibernate internally follows these steps:

  1. Fetch entity from database 
    Employee employee = repository.findById(101L).get();
  2. Hibernate stores the original state (Snapshot) 
    id = 101
name = Rahul
salary = 30000
  3. Modify entity 
    employee.setSalary(50000);
  4. Hibernate compares entity with snapshot
  5. Original salary: 30000
  6. Current salary: 50000
  7. Difference detected!
  8. Hibernate generates UPDATE SQL 
    UPDATE employee
SET salary = 50000
WHERE id = 101;
  9. Transaction commits
  10. Changes are persisted in the database.

docs.title: Employee.java
docs.text:
@Entity
@Table(name = "employee")
public class Employee {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private String name;

    private double salary;

    // Getters and Setters
}

docs.title: EmployeeRepository.java
docs.text:
@Repository
public interface EmployeeRepository extends JpaRepository<Employee, Long> {
}

docs.title: EmployeeService.java
docs.text:
@Service
public class EmployeeService {

    private final EmployeeRepository employeeRepository;

    public EmployeeService(EmployeeRepository employeeRepository) {
        this.employeeRepository = employeeRepository;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void updateSalary(Long employeeId) {

        // Step 1: Fetch employee from database.
        // Hibernate makes this entity managed.
        Employee employee = employeeRepository
                .findById(employeeId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException("Employee not found"));

        // Step 2: Modify the managed entity.
        // Hibernate detects this modification automatically.
        employee.setSalary(50000);

        // Step 3: No repository.save() required!
        // Hibernate detects changes during flush/commit.
    }
}

Important: save() is not required here because the entity is already managed by the persistence context.

docs.title: 1.4 Managed vs Detached Entity
docs.text:
Dirty checking works only on managed entities.

Entity State Dirty Checking? Transient No Managed Yes Detached No Removed No normal update tracking

Managed Example: 

@Transactional
public void updateEmployee() {
    Employee employee = employeeRepository.findById(101L).get();

    // Managed entity
    employee.setName("Rahul Kumar");

    // Dirty checking detects this change.
}

Detached Example: 

Employee employee = employeeRepository.findById(101L).get();

// Entity is detached after its persistence context closes.
employee.setName("Rahul Kumar");

// No automatic dirty checking here.

docs.title: 1.5 When does Hibernate execute UPDATE?
docs.text:
An important interview point: Hibernate generally checks entity changes during flush.

Flush can happen: - Before transaction commit. - When EntityManager.flush() is called. - Automatically before certain queries, depending on flush mode.

Remember: Flush is not the same as commit. - Flush sends pending SQL statements to the database. - Commit completes the database transaction.

docs.title: 1.6 Interview Questions (Dirty Checking)
docs.text:
Q1. Is save() mandatory when updating an existing entity? No. If the entity is managed within an active persistence context, Hibernate automatically detects modifications through dirty checking.

Q2. Does dirty checking work for detached entities? No. Detached entities are not tracked by the current persistence context.

Q3. Does dirty checking execute UPDATE immediately? No. Hibernate normally detects changes during flush and executes SQL then.

Q4. How can we improve dirty checking performance? - Avoid unnecessarily loading large numbers of entities. - Use read-only transactions (@Transactional(readOnly = true)) for read-only operations. - Use appropriate batch processing. - Use DTO projections when entity management is unnecessary.

docs.title: 2. Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking
docs.text:
These concepts are used to handle concurrent database updates.

The Scenario: Imagine two users trying to update the same bank account balance simultaneously: - Initial account balance: ₹10,000 - User A: Withdraw ₹3,000 - User B: Withdraw ₹5,000

Both users read ₹10,000 at almost the same time. Without proper concurrency control, both transactions may overwrite each other's changes. This is called the Lost Update Problem.

There are two common solutions: 1. Optimistic Locking 2. Pessimistic Locking

docs.title: 2.1 Optimistic Locking
docs.text: Optimistic Locking assumes that conflicts are rare. It allows multiple transactions to read the same record but checks for conflicting updates when they write. It commonly uses a @Version field.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
Suppose the database contains:

id balance version 101 10000 0

Optimistic Locking Workflow: 1. Transaction A reads balance = 10000, version = 0 2. Transaction B reads balance = 10000, version = 0 3. Transaction A updates successfully: 

UPDATE account
SET balance = 7000,
    version = 1
WHERE id = 101
  AND version = 0;
-- Result: 1 row updated
4. Transaction B tries to update: 
UPDATE account
SET balance = 5000,
    version = 1
WHERE id = 101
  AND version = 0;
-- Result: 0 rows updated
Version is now 1, not 0. Hibernate detects the conflict and throws an optimistic locking exception. Transaction B must reload the latest balance and retry or return a conflict response.

docs.title: Account.java
docs.text:
@Entity
@Table(name = "account")
public class Account {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private double balance;

    // Hibernate maintains this version automatically.
    @Version
    private Integer version;

    // Getters and Setters
}

docs.title: AccountService.java
docs.text:
@Service
public class AccountService {

    private final AccountRepository accountRepository;

    public AccountService(AccountRepository accountRepository) {
        this.accountRepository = accountRepository;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void withdraw(Long accountId, double amount) {

        // Fetch account and its current version.
        Account account = accountRepository
                .findById(accountId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException("Account not found"));

        if (account.getBalance() < amount) {
            throw new RuntimeException("Insufficient balance");
        }

        // Modify the managed entity.
        account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - amount);

        // Hibernate checks the version during flush/commit.
        // If another transaction updated the record,
        // an optimistic locking exception is thrown.
    }
}

Note: You don't need to manually increment the version. Hibernate handles it. Exception to know: ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException (Spring can translate the underlying Hibernate optimistic locking exception into this exception).

docs.title: When should you use Optimistic Locking?
docs.text:
• Multiple users update the same data occasionally.
  • Conflicts are relatively rare.
  • You don't want to lock database records while users are reading.
  • High-read applications.
  • Inventory or account update operations where version conflicts should be detected.

docs.title: 2.2 Pessimistic Locking
docs.text: Pessimistic Locking assumes that conflicts may occur. It locks the database record so that competing transactions cannot modify it concurrently. Instead of detecting a conflict after an update, it prevents competing updates by acquiring a database lock first.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
Initial database:

id balance 101 10000

Pessimistic Locking Workflow: 1. Transaction A reads account using SELECT FOR UPDATE: 

SELECT * FROM account
WHERE id = 101
FOR UPDATE;
-- Exclusive row lock acquired
2. Transaction B tries to acquire the same row lock: - Must wait. It cannot acquire the conflicting lock until Transaction A releases it. 3. Transaction A commits: - Balance becomes ₹7,000. Lock is released. 4. Transaction B continues: - Reads the updated balance of ₹7,000 and performs its operation against the latest state.

docs.title: AccountRepository.java
docs.text:
@Repository
public interface AccountRepository extends JpaRepository<Account, Long> {

    // Acquire a database write lock when fetching the account.
    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
    @Query("SELECT a FROM Account a WHERE a.id = :id")
    Optional<Account> findByIdWithLock(@Param("id") Long id);
}

docs.title: AccountService.java
docs.text:
@Service
public class AccountService {

    private final AccountRepository accountRepository;

    public AccountService(AccountRepository accountRepository) {
        this.accountRepository = accountRepository;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void withdraw(Long accountId, double amount) {

        // Fetch account with a database-level lock.
        Account account = accountRepository
                .findByIdWithLock(accountId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException("Account not found"));

        if (account.getBalance() < amount) {
            throw new RuntimeException("Insufficient balance");
        }

        // Other transactions requesting conflicting locks
        // must wait until this transaction completes.
        account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - amount);
    }
}

Hibernate typically generates SQL similar to (exact SQL depends on the database): 

SELECT *
FROM account
WHERE id = 101
FOR UPDATE;

docs.title: Types of Pessimistic Locking
docs.text: Lock Type Meaning PESSIMISTIC_READ Acquires a shared/read lock where supported PESSIMISTIC_WRITE Acquires an exclusive/write lock PESSIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT Acquires a lock and forces version increment for versioned entities

docs.title: When should you use Pessimistic Locking?
docs.text:
• High contention on the same database record.
  • Critical inventory updates.
  • Financial operations requiring serialized access.
  • Multiple transactions frequently update the same row.

Be careful: Pessimistic locks can cause blocking, deadlocks, and reduced throughput.

docs.title: 3. Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking – Comparison
docs.text: Feature Optimistic Pessimistic Approach Detect conflict Prevent conflict Mechanism @Version Database locks Lock acquired No long-held row lock Yes Concurrent reads Allowed Generally allowed depending on lock Conflict handling Exception Waiting or timeout Performance Better with rare conflicts Can reduce throughput Deadlock risk Lower Higher Best for Low contention High contention

docs.title: 4. Real-World Banking Example
docs.text: Suppose you are developing a banking application with two scenarios:

docs.title: Scenario A: Updating customer profile
docs.text: Two users might occasionally update a customer's address. - Choice: Use Optimistic Locking. - Why? - Conflicts are rare. - No need to block other transactions. - If a conflict occurs, notify the user to refresh.

docs.title: Scenario B: Withdrawing money from an account
docs.text: Multiple transactions may try to withdraw money from the same account. - Choice: Pessimistic Locking can be useful when contention is high and you need to serialize access to the account row. - Note: However, Optimistic Locking with proper atomic database updates and transaction handling can also work well. The correct choice depends on contention and consistency requirements.

docs.title: 5. Important Interview Questions
docs.text:
Test your understanding by answering these questions:

  1. Q1. What is dirty checking in Hibernate?
  2. Q2. Is repository.save() required when updating a managed entity?
  3. Q3. What is @Version in JPA?
  4. Q4. What happens when two transactions update the same versioned entity?
  5. Q5. Does pessimistic locking block SELECT queries?
  6. Q6. Can optimistic locking prevent lost updates?
  7. Q7. Which locking strategy is better for banking applications?

docs.title: 6. Final Revision Notes
docs.text:
Remember these four points for interviews: 1. Dirty Checking: Automatically detects modifications in managed entities. 2. Persistence Context: Maintains managed entities and their snapshots. 3. Optimistic Locking: Uses @Version to detect concurrent modifications. 4. Pessimistic Locking: Uses database locks to control concurrent access.

Recommendation: Practice all three concepts together using a Bank Account application. Implement dirty checking, then optimistic locking with @Version, and finally pessimistic locking with PESSIMISTIC_WRITE. This gives you a strong practical answer for a Senior Java Backend interview.

docs.title: Idempotency – 7 Important Microservices Interview Questions & Answers
docs.text:
These are important follow-up questions for a Java Backend Developer interview, especially when working on banking, wallet, fund transfer, and payment microservices.

Each question is explained in simple language with: * Easy explanation * Real-world payment example * Spring Boot implementation approach * Interview-ready answer

docs.title: 1. What is idempotency in REST APIs?
Easy Explanation
docs.text:
Idempotency means performing the same operation multiple times produces the same final result as performing it once.

For example: A customer sends a payment request to transfer ₹5,000. * First request: ₹5,000 is deducted. * Second request: No additional deduction. * Third request: No additional deduction.

The final result remains the same.

docs.title: HTTP Methods and Idempotency
docs.text:
HTTP Method Idempotent? Explanation GET Yes Reading data does not change server state PUT Yes Replacing a resource with the same data gives the same result DELETE Yes Deleting an already deleted resource has the same final state POST Usually no Repeated requests may create multiple records PATCH Depends Depends on the operation being performed

Example: 

PUT /api/accounts/101
{
  "accountHolder": "Praveen",
  "status": "ACTIVE"
}
Sending this request multiple times produces the same final account state.

However, with a POST request: 

POST /api/payments
Sending it multiple times could create multiple payments unless we implement idempotency.

docs.title: Interview-Ready Answer
docs.text: "Idempotency means that executing the same API request multiple times produces the same final result as executing it once. In payment applications, I implement idempotency using a unique idempotency key. If the client retries a request, the server identifies the duplicate and returns the previously stored result instead of processing the payment again."

docs.title: 2. What happens if two identical requests arrive simultaneously?
docs.text: (Important concurrency question)

docs.title: Easy Explanation
docs.text:
Suppose a client sends the same payment request twice at almost the same time, and both requests reach the server.

Consider this scenario:

Time Request 1 Request 2 T1 Checks key T2 Key not found T3 Checks key T4 Key not found T5 Processes payment T6 Processes payment

Both requests see that the key does not exist. This is called a race condition. As a result, both requests may process the payment.

docs.title: How do we prevent it?
docs.text:
Use a database unique constraint.

CREATE TABLE idempotency_records (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    idempotency_key VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(30),
    response_body TEXT,
    UNIQUE (idempotency_key)
);

Now, if two requests try to insert the same key: * Request 1 inserts successfully. * Request 2 gets a duplicate-key error. * Request 2 does not process the payment.

docs.title: Spring Boot Approach
docs.text:
@Transactional
public PaymentResponse processPayment(
        String key,
        PaymentRequest request) {

    try {
        // Atomically reserve the idempotency key.
        repository.insertInProgress(key);

    } catch (DuplicateKeyException ex) {

        // Another request already owns this key.
        return handleExistingRequest(key);
    }

    // Only the request that successfully reserved
    // the key can execute the payment.
    return executePayment(request);
}

Note: insertInProgress() should use an atomic database insert, not a separate check followed by insert.

Production Note: Be careful with transaction boundaries. Depending on the database and isolation level, a competing insert may wait for the first transaction to commit or roll back. Handle that outcome and read the existing record in a suitable transaction.

docs.title: Interview-Ready Answer
docs.text: "If two identical requests arrive simultaneously, a simple database check is not sufficient because both requests might find that the key does not exist. I prevent this using a unique constraint on the idempotency key and an atomic insert operation. Only one request can reserve the key and process the payment. The other request either waits for the first transaction or receives a duplicate-key response and returns the existing payment result."

docs.title: 3. What if the server crashes after deducting money but before saving the idempotency record?
docs.text: (Very important banking scenario)

docs.title: Easy Explanation
docs.text:
Suppose: 1. Client sends a ₹5,000 payment. 2. Server deducts ₹5,000. 3. Server crashes. 4. Idempotency record is not saved. 5. Client retries the request. 6. Server thinks it is a new request. 7. Another ₹5,000 may be deducted.

This is a serious problem.

docs.title: Solution 1: Database Transaction
docs.text:
If the payment deduction and idempotency record are stored in the same database, use one transaction.

@Transactional
public PaymentResponse processPayment(
        String key,
        PaymentRequest request) {

    // Reserve idempotency key.
    repository.insertInProgress(key);

    // Deduct money.
    accountRepository.debit(
            request.getFromAccount(),
            request.getAmount()
    );

    // Create payment transaction.
    paymentRepository.save(createPayment(request));

    // Update idempotency result.
    repository.markSuccess(
            key,
            "Payment successful"
    );

    return new PaymentResponse("SUCCESS");
}

What happens if the application crashes before commit? In a single database transaction: 1. Reserve idempotency key. 2. Deduct account balance. 3. Save payment record. 4. Save successful response. 5. Commit transaction (All changes committed together).

If the transaction fails before commit, all its database changes are rolled back.

docs.title: Solution 2: What if an external payment gateway is involved?
docs.text:
A database transaction cannot automatically roll back an external payment gateway transaction.

For example: * Your service calls an external bank. * The bank successfully deducts money. * Your application crashes before recording the result.

In this case, use: 1. A unique payment reference. 2. The gateway's idempotency key, if supported. 3. Payment status reconciliation. 4. Gateway transaction status inquiry. 5. Retry using the same reference, not a new payment reference.

If the outcome is unknown, mark the payment as UNKNOWN or PENDING_RECONCILIATION rather than blindly retrying the debit.

docs.title: Interview-Ready Answer
docs.text: "I would handle this using database transactions if the account deduction and idempotency record belong to the same database. Both operations should commit or roll back together. However, if an external payment gateway is involved, a local database transaction cannot guarantee rollback of the external payment. In that case, I use a unique transaction reference, gateway-level idempotency, and reconciliation to verify the payment status before retrying."

docs.title: 4. How do you handle IN_PROGRESS payment requests?
Easy Explanation
docs.text:
Suppose the first request is still processing, and the client sends the same request again. We need to identify whether the payment is: * Still processing. * Successfully completed. * Failed.

For this, maintain payment states.

docs.title: Payment Status Lifecycle
docs.text:
• IN_PROGRESS: Payment request reserved and processing
  • SUCCESS: Return saved response
  • FAILED: Return failure result

docs.title: How to Handle Duplicate Requests
docs.text:
Existing Status Server Action IN_PROGRESS Return HTTP 202 Accepted or a suitable processing response SUCCESS Return previously saved successful response FAILED Return saved failure response or follow defined retry policy UNKNOWN Check payment status before taking further action

Example Response (HTTP 202 Accepted): 

{
  "paymentId": "PAY1001",
  "status": "IN_PROGRESS",
  "message": "Payment is being processed"
}

The client can check payment status using: 

GET /api/payments/PAY1001/status

Important: Don't automatically change an old IN_PROGRESS record to FAILED just because a timeout occurred. The payment might have succeeded externally.

docs.title: Interview-Ready Answer
docs.text: "I maintain payment states such as IN_PROGRESS, SUCCESS, FAILED and UNKNOWN. When a duplicate request arrives, I check the existing status. If it is IN_PROGRESS, I return a processing response instead of executing the payment again. If it is SUCCESS, I return the saved response. For uncertain outcomes, I verify the actual payment status before retrying."

docs.title: 5. What is the difference between idempotency and duplicate request validation?
Easy Explanation
docs.text: Both prevent unwanted duplicate operations, but they solve different problems. * Duplicate request validation: Checks whether a request is invalid or duplicated according to business rules. * Idempotency: Ensures that retrying the same logical operation does not execute it again and returns the previous result.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Suppose a customer transfers ₹5,000. * Duplicate validation: The customer submits the same payment twice because of a double-click. The application checks whether the same transaction reference already exists. * Idempotency: The payment is already processed, but the client did not receive the response due to a network timeout. The client retries with the same idempotency key. The server returns the previous payment result.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Feature Duplicate Validation Idempotency Main purpose Detect duplicate business operations Safely handle retries Identification Business rules or transaction reference Idempotency key Previous response Not necessarily returned Usually returned Retry support Not necessarily Yes Example Prevent duplicate order Prevent duplicate payment

docs.title: Spring Boot Example
docs.text:
Duplicate validation: 

if (paymentRepository.existsByTransactionReference(
        request.getTransactionReference())) {

    throw new DuplicatePaymentException(
            "Payment already exists"
    );
}

Idempotency: 

var existing = repository.findByIdempotencyKey(key);
if (existing.isPresent()) {
    return existing.get().getResponseBody();
}

docs.title: Interview-Ready Answer
docs.text: "Duplicate request validation checks whether an operation violates business rules, such as creating the same order twice. Idempotency is different because it handles client retries safely. For example, if a payment succeeds but the response times out, the client can retry with the same idempotency key, and the server returns the previous response without executing the payment again."

docs.title: 6. How do you implement idempotency in a microservices architecture?
docs.text: (Important system design question)

docs.title: Easy Explanation
docs.text:
Suppose we have a banking application with multiple microservices: * Client: Payment request + Idempotency Key * API Gateway: Authentication and routing * Payment Service: Idempotency check, payment reference, and transaction status * Account Service: Debit / Credit * Notification Service: Payment notification

Each service protects its own operations against duplicate processing.

docs.title: Practical Implementation
docs.text: Consider a ₹5,000 transfer from Account A to Account B.

docs.title: Step 1: Client sends the request
docs.text:
POST /api/payments
Idempotency-Key: PAYMENT-101

docs.title: Step 2: Payment Service
docs.text:
• Checks the idempotency key.
  • Creates a payment record.
  • Stores the payment reference.
  • Coordinates the payment workflow.

docs.title: Step 3: Account Service
docs.text:
The Payment Service sends a debit command: 

{
  "transactionId": "PAYMENT-101",
  "accountId": "ACC101",
  "amount": 5000,
  "operation": "DEBIT"
}
The Account Service maintains its own transaction reference with a unique constraint. If the same debit command arrives again, it does not debit the account twice.

docs.title: Step 4: Notification Service
docs.text:
Suppose Kafka delivers the same payment-success event twice. The Notification Service maintains a processed-event table: 

CREATE TABLE processed_events (
    event_id VARCHAR(100) PRIMARY KEY,
    processed_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
If the event ID already exists, the consumer skips processing it again.

docs.title: Important Microservices Concepts
docs.text: Concept Purpose Idempotency key Identifies the original client request Unique transaction ID Prevents duplicate business operations Database unique constraint Handles concurrent duplicate requests Kafka event ID Identifies duplicate messages Inbox pattern Tracks consumed messages Outbox pattern Reliably publishes database changes as events Saga pattern Coordinates distributed business transactions Reconciliation Resolves uncertain payment outcomes

docs.title: What about the Saga pattern?
docs.text:
In microservices, each service has its own database. We generally cannot use one local @Transactional transaction across all services.

For example: 1. Payment Service initiates payment. 2. Account Service debits money. 3. Another operation credits the beneficiary. 4. Notification Service sends confirmation.

If a later step fails, the Saga pattern coordinates compensating actions where appropriate. Idempotency is still required in each service because messages and commands may be delivered more than once.

docs.title: Interview-Ready Answer
docs.text: "In a microservices architecture, I implement idempotency at multiple levels. The Payment Service maintains an idempotency key for incoming API requests. The Account Service uses a unique transaction reference to prevent duplicate debit or credit operations. For Kafka consumers, I use event IDs and an inbox or processed-event table to avoid duplicate message processing. I also use the transactional outbox pattern to reliably publish events and Saga for coordinating distributed transactions. This ensures that retries and duplicate messages do not result in duplicate business operations."

docs.title: 7. How do you handle retries using Resilience4j?
docs.text: (Relevant to Spring Boot microservices)

docs.title: Easy Explanation
docs.text:
Sometimes a service fails temporarily because of: * Network problems. * Temporary database connectivity issues. * Another microservice being unavailable. * Gateway timeout.

Instead of immediately failing, we retry the operation.

For example: Payment Service calls Account Service. The first request fails because of a temporary network issue, so the Payment Service retries the request. However, retrying a payment without idempotency can cause duplicate deductions. Therefore, we combine Resilience4j Retry with idempotency.

Request Flow: 1. Payment Service triggers Resilience4j Retry (Maximum 3 attempts). 2. Calls Account Service using the same transaction ID for every retry. 3. Database uses a unique transaction ID to prevent duplicate debits.

docs.title: Step 1: Add Maven Dependency
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.resilience4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>resilience4j-spring-boot3</artifactId>
</dependency>
(Use the appropriate compatible Resilience4j version through your dependency management or Spring Boot dependency configuration.)

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Retry (application.yml)
docs.text:
resilience4j:
  retry:
    instances:
      accountService:
        max-attempts: 3
        wait-duration: 2s
        enable-exponential-backoff: true
        exponential-backoff-multiplier: 2
Setting Meaning max-attempts Maximum 3 total attempts wait-duration Initial wait of 2 seconds exponential backoff Increase wait time after each failure multiplier Double the wait duration

docs.title: Step 3: Apply Retry Annotation
docs.text:
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentService {

    private final AccountClient accountClient;

    @Retry(name = "accountService")
    public String debitAccount(
            String transactionId,
            BigDecimal amount) {

        return accountClient.debit(
                transactionId,
                amount
        );
    }
}
Every retry must use the same transactionId.

docs.title: Step 4: Protect Account Service
docs.text:
@Transactional
public String debitAccount(
        String transactionId,
        BigDecimal amount) {

    // Check whether this transaction was already processed.
    if (repository.existsByTransactionId(transactionId)) {
        return "Already processed";
    }

    // Perform the debit and save the transaction
    // atomically in the same database transaction.
    accountRepository.debit(amount);

    repository.save(
        new AccountTransaction(transactionId, amount)
    );

    return "Debit successful";
}
(For production, use an atomic reservation or database unique constraint on transactionId; a simple existence check alone is not safe under concurrency.)

docs.title: Step 5: What happens during retry?
docs.text: Attempt Account Service Result 1 Debit successful, response times out 2 Same transaction ID received 3 Already processed; return previous result Final Result Only ₹5,000 is deducted, even though the service receives three requests.

docs.title: Important Production Considerations
docs.text:
1. Retry only transient failures, such as selected network errors and temporary service unavailability.
  2. Do not retry business failures such as insufficient balance.
  3. Reuse the same idempotency key or transaction ID on every attempt.
  4. Use exponential backoff and jitter to avoid overwhelming the downstream service.
  5. Configure a Circuit Breaker to stop repeated calls when a service is unhealthy.
  6. Be careful with timeouts: a timeout does not mean the downstream operation failed.
  7. Avoid retrying at multiple layers without a retry budget, because retries can multiply.

docs.title: Interview-Ready Answer
docs.text: "In Spring Boot microservices, I use Resilience4j Retry to handle temporary failures when communicating with downstream services. I configure maximum attempts, wait duration and exponential backoff. However, for payment operations, retry alone is not sufficient. I pass the same transaction ID or idempotency key with every retry. The downstream Account Service checks that transaction ID and prevents duplicate debit operations. I also configure Circuit Breaker and retry only transient failures. This ensures reliable communication without executing the same payment multiple times."

docs.title: Final Revision – Remember These 7 Concepts
docs.text: Question Key Concept to Remember 1. What is idempotency? Same operation, same final result 2. Simultaneous requests? Unique constraint + atomic insert 3. Server crashes? Database transaction + reconciliation 4. IN_PROGRESS handling? Payment state management 5. Idempotency vs validation? Safe retries vs business duplicate checks 6. Microservices implementation? Idempotency + Inbox + Outbox + Saga 7. Resilience4j retries? Retry + backoff + same transaction ID

docs.title: Important Concepts to Prepare Next
docs.text:
These concepts are closely connected to payment reliability and are frequently discussed in senior Java backend interviews: 1. Database: ACID properties, transaction isolation, optimistic and pessimistic locking. 2. Concurrency: Race conditions, atomic operations, distributed locks. 3. Microservices: Saga, Outbox, Inbox, eventual consistency. 4. Kafka: At-least-once delivery, duplicate messages, consumer idempotency. 5. Resilience4j: Retry, Circuit Breaker, Rate Limiter, Bulkhead, TimeLimiter.

One important interview lesson: Idempotency does not mean a request executes only once at the network level. It means the business operation produces its intended effect only once, even when requests or messages are delivered multiple times.

docs.title: Spring Boot Database Connection Exhaustion: Production Troubleshooting Guide
docs.text:
This is a very common Spring Boot production performance issue, especially in microservices and banking applications.

The first thing I would investigate is why database connections are not being released or why all connections are busy for too long.

Let's understand it step by step.

docs.title: 1. Understand the Problem
docs.text:
Suppose your Spring Boot application normally responds in 200 ms. Suddenly, in production: * API response time increases to 5–10 seconds. * CPU usage is normal. * Database connections are exhausted. * New API requests are waiting for database connections.

Imagine your application has a maximum of 10 database connections.

docs.title: Example: Database Connection Pool
docs.text:
Metric Value Maximum connections 10 Currently busy 10 / 10 Available connections 0

All 10 connections are occupied. New requests must wait until a connection becomes available, and this waiting period increases API response time.

docs.title: 2. What Would I Investigate First?
docs.text: I would investigate these five things, in this order:

docs.title: 1. Connection Leaks
docs.text:
Question: Are database connections being released properly?

Bad Example (Connection Leak): 

Connection connection = dataSource.getConnection();

// Execute database operation

// Connection is not closed!
If connections are not released, they remain occupied indefinitely.

Correct Approach: 

try (Connection connection = dataSource.getConnection()) {

    // Execute database operation

} // Connection automatically closes here

Note: In Spring Data JPA, Spring normally manages connections for you. I would check custom JDBC code and manual transaction handling.

docs.title: 2. Long-Running Database Queries
docs.text:
Question: Are SQL queries taking too much time?

Example: 

SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 101;
* Previously: Execution time was 20 ms. * Now: Because of missing indexes or increased data volume, execution time is 5 seconds.

The connection remains occupied while the query executes. To resolve this, I would check: * Slow SQL queries. * Missing database indexes. * Database execution plans (EXPLAIN). * Database locks.

docs.title: 3. Long-Running Transactions
docs.text:
Question: Are transactions staying open for too long?

Example: 

@Transactional
public void transferMoney() {

    Account account = accountRepository.findById(1L)
            .orElseThrow();

    // Database transaction remains open.

    callExternalPaymentService(); // Takes 5 seconds

    account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - 1000);

}
Here, the application makes an external API call while the database transaction is open, holding a database connection unnecessarily. I would move external API calls outside the database transaction where the business flow allows it.

docs.title: 4. Connection Pool Configuration
docs.text:
Spring Boot commonly uses HikariCP. I would check the following properties in application.properties or application.yml:

spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=30000
spring.datasource.hikari.leak-detection-threshold=20000

I would monitor: * Active connections * Idle connections * Pending connection requests * Connection acquisition time * Connection timeout errors

Best Practice: I would not immediately increase the pool size without understanding the root cause.

docs.title: 5. Database Performance and Locks
docs.text: I would check whether: * Database CPU or memory is overloaded. * Other queries are blocking transactions. * Database locks or deadlocks are causing waiting. * Maximum database connections on the DB server itself are reached.

docs.title: 3. What Tools Would I Use?
docs.text: Tool What I Investigate Spring Boot Actuator Application health and metrics HikariCP Metrics Active, idle, and pending connections Grafana Connection usage trends over time Prometheus Connection pool metrics scraping Kibana / ELK Errors and slow application logs Database Monitoring Slow queries, execution plans, and locks

docs.title: 4. How Would I Explain This in an Interview?
Interview-Ready Answer
docs.text:
"I would first investigate database connection pool exhaustion rather than CPU usage because the application is likely waiting for database connections.

I would check HikariCP metrics, especially active connections, idle connections, and pending threads. Then I would investigate possible connection leaks, slow SQL queries, long-running transactions, and database locks.

For example, if an API makes an external service call inside a @Transactional method, the database connection might remain occupied while waiting for the external service.

I would use Spring Boot Actuator, Prometheus, and Grafana to identify the bottleneck, and I would fix the root cause first instead of blindly increasing the connection pool size."

docs.title: Springboot
docs.text:
1. API suddenly becomes slow
  2. Duplicate payment after client retry
  3. @Transactional doesn't roll back
  4. Hibernate N+1 query problem
  5. One Spring Boot instance suddenly runs out of memory
  6. Two users update the same database row
  7. Application works locally but times out in production
  8. Third-party API becomes slow
  9. @Async is not working asynchronously
  10. Choosing the right caching strategy
  11. Kafka delivers duplicate messages
  12. API needs to return 100,000+ records
  13. JVM CPU reaches 95%
  14. Circular dependency in Spring Boot
  15. Zero-downtime deployment
